slots.hypothesis: Axis B: how many distinct minute-return values a stock takes, relative to its size peers. Mechanically this mixes three channels (Harris 1991): relative tick, trading activity and intraday range. H2 (sign -1) agrees in direction with the LOT/Amihud illiquidity-level premium, but it only conditions on size, so the turnover and volatility parts can leak back through a saturating function (traps 1/3). Periphery: (1) DGTW-style sequential matching on unadjusted price (Holden 2009), same-day turnover, intraday volatility and zero-return share; (2) multi-day levels (cross_mean, cross_ema, median) instead of ts_max peaks, plus an Amihud level-vs-shock split written as time-series differences; (3) screens that push frozen/limit-locked names and the smallest 20% by cap out of the long leg (Liu-Stambaugh-Yuan). 13 seeds. Expected to persist out of sample if what survives the matching is the transaction cost itself; if it does not survive, axis B is a control rewrite.

Intraday return asymmetry, i.e. lottery demand. Under Barberis-Huang 2008 probability weighting, positively skewed stocks are overpriced; Amaya et al. 2015 find 5-minute realized skewness predicts returns negatively, and Bollerslev-Li-Zhao 2020 find the same with the relative signed jump (RV+ - RV-)/RV. Returns exclude the opening and closing auctions (in_slice), and 5-minute aggregation suppresses the 0.01-yuan tick-grid noise that axis B showed dominates minute statistics. Seeds: skew and RSJ (20/60-day mean, EMA); ranked within deciles of unadjusted price, 20-day return (to remove the overlap with the reversal control), volatility and turnover; a screen pushing names stuck at the day's low (limit-down locks) out of the long leg; a daily-skew comparison. 13 seeds. Expected |rho| < 0.3 with all 6 heads, which sit on two axes only (size and tick-grid staleness).
